results.result: The MEC-13-53D transgenic mouse line specifically targets excitatory LVb neurons in both LEC and MEC. mCherry-positive neurons were predominantly found in LVb (93.2% in LEC, 82.9% in MEC), with minimal expression in LVa (1.7% in LEC, 0.3% in MEC) and superficial layers. The line shows high specificity with 91.7% (LEC) and 99.3% (MEC) of tTA-expressing neurons being PCP4-positive, and low colocalization with GAD67 (4.3% in LEC, 2.3% in MEC), confirming targeting of excitatory neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C33 provide comprehensive characterization of the transgenic line with quantitative data from immunohistochemistry and colocalization studies. The data consistently demonstrate specificity for LVb excitatory neurons across multiple markers (PCP4, Ctip2, GAD67), with appropriate statistical comparisons and controls. The conclusion that this is a suitable line for targeting excitatory LVb neurons is well-supported by the presented evidence.

results.result: LVb neurons in MEC and LEC exhibit distinct morphological properties. MEC-LVb neurons have apical dendrites extending to layer I, while LEC-LVb dendrites do not extend beyond layer III. This morphological difference suggests LEC-LVb neurons are unlikely to receive inputs from layers I and II (such as olfactory inputs). Electrophysiologically, MEC-LVb neurons show shorter time constants than LEC-LVb neurons, indicating a shorter time window for input integration.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C38 are supported by morphological reconstructions (Figure 1G-J) and electrophysiological measurements (Figure 2). The morphological observations are corroborated by in vivo labeling (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) ruling out slicing artifacts. The functional inference about input integration (C38) is appropriately supported by citations and the time constant data (C37).

results.result: LVb and LVa neurons can be distinguished by electrophysiological properties. LVa neurons show smaller sag ratio and AP frequency but larger time constant compared to LVb neurons. Within LVb, MEC neurons show smaller time constant, higher AP frequency, and smaller fast AHP than LEC neurons. In contrast, LVa neurons in MEC and LEC are electrophysiologically similar.
results.evaluation: Claims C55, C58-C60, and C54 are supported by comprehensive electrophysiological characterization of 121 neurons with statistical analysis (Figure 2, one-way ANOVA with post-hoc tests). Principal component analysis confirms the separation between cell types. The data are internally consistent and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: Anatomical tracing reveals striking differences in LVb-to-LVa connectivity between LEC and MEC. Many labeled axons from LEC-LVb neurons were present in LVa, whereas MEC-LVb showed very low axonal labeling in LVa. Quantitatively, normalized labeling was significantly higher in LEC-LVa than MEC-LVa (p=0.0003), while LII labeling was similar between regions (p=0.82). This indicates stronger connections from LVb-to-LVa neurons in dorsal LEC compared to dorsal MEC.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 and C5, C21, C56-C57 are supported by viral tracing experiments with quantitative analysis (Figure 3). The findings are corroborated by multiple approaches including PCP4 labeling patterns and anterograde tracing in wild-type mice and rats (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). Statistical analysis with paired t-tests is appropriate. The consistency across methods strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of MEC-LVb fibers revealed differential connectivity patterns. All LIII neurons (30/30) responded to stimulation. In LII, 61.1% of pyramidal neurons but only 25.0% of stellate cells responded. Only 27.8% of LVa neurons responded. The normalized EPSP of LEC-LVa neurons (0.93±0.10) was significantly larger than MEC-LVa neurons (0.47±0.10, p<0.05), confirming anatomical findings of stronger LVb-to-LVa connectivity in LEC.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46, C49-C50 are supported by optogenetic experiments with whole-cell recordings (Figure 4). Response probabilities and amplitudes are quantified with appropriate statistics. The functional data corroborate the anatomical findings. Controls for technical artifacts (oChIEF expression levels, dendritic severing) are provided in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

results.result: In LEC, optogenetic stimulation revealed high response probabilities in LIIb (76.9%), LIII (100%), and LVa (94.7%), but low in LIIa fan cells (26.9%). EPSP latencies were similar across all cell types (4.2-5.0 ms), suggesting largely monosynaptic connectivity. The small responses of LIIa fan cells cannot be explained by input resistance differences (fan cells had significantly higher input resistance than LIIb/LIII neurons, p<0.001) and likely reflect fewer synaptic inputs from LVb.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C48, C72-C76 are supported by optogenetic experiments in LEC (Figure 5). The latency analysis (C72) appropriately supports the monosynaptic interpretation (C73), consistent with previous rabies tracing (Ohara et al., 2018). The input resistance analysis (C74) properly rules out a biophysical explanation for small fan cell responses (C75), making the anatomical explanation (C76) reasonable though speculative.

results.result: LVb neurons in both LEC and MEC preferentially target pyramidal neurons in LIII and LII rather than stellate/fan cells. This connectivity pattern is similar between the two entorhinal subdivisions. The findings suggest hippocampal information preferentially interacts with the LIII-to-CA1/Sub projection system rather than the LII-to-DG/CA2-3 system.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41, C22 are supported by both anatomical (Figure 3) and electrophysiological data (Figures 4-5). The preferential targeting of pyramidal over stellate/fan cells is demonstrated by response probabilities and normalized EPSPs. The inference about hippocampal information flow (C41) is reasonable given the connectivity patterns, though it remains to be tested in vivo.

results.result: In MEC, LVb-to-LVa connectivity shows dorsoventral differences. Voltage responses of ventrally positioned LVa neurons were significantly higher than dorsal ones (p<0.01). This difference is not due to varying oChIEF expression (LIII responses were similar across levels) or dendritic severing (dorsal LVa cells with intact dendrites still did not respond). In ventral MEC, 4/5 neurons with intact dendrites responded.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by systematic analysis across dorsoventral levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The controls for technical artifacts (oChIEF expression, dendritic integrity) are appropriate. The data suggest genuine regional differences in connectivity, though the sample sizes for some conditions are small (n=3-5 for intact dendrites).

results.result: In MEC, EPSP onset latencies differed across cell types. LII stellate cells showed significantly longer latencies than LIII cells (4.3±0.7 vs. 2.9±0.1 ms, p<0.05), while LII pyramidal cells had similar latencies to LIII (3.2±0.2 vs. 2.9±0.1 ms). LVa cells showed significantly longer latencies than LIII (5.6±1.7 vs. 2.9±0.1 ms, p<0.001), suggesting monosynaptic inputs to apical dendrites in LIII or disynaptic responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by latency measurements with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 4H). The interpretation of mono- vs. disynaptic connectivity based on latencies is reasonable, though the authors acknowledge lack of pharmacological validation. The longer latencies for stellate and LVa cells are consistent with the anatomical observations of sparse connectivity.

results.result: The weak LVb-to-LVa projection in dorsal MEC is not due to technical issues but reflects genuine circuit differences. The intrinsic LV circuitry underlying the canonical hippocampal-cortical output circuit in dorsal MEC is differently organized than in other parts of EC.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C52 are supported by consistency across multiple experimental approaches (viral tracing, optogenetics, PCP4 labeling) and appropriate controls ruling out technical artifacts. The conclusion is further supported by corroborating evidence from independent studies (Rozov et al., 2020) and previous tracing data in rats and monkeys.

results.result: The differential LVb-to-LVa connectivity between LEC and MEC suggests different operating principles in these regions and implies potential differences in how they mediate episodic systems consolidation. LEC might be more relevant than MEC in mediating hippocampal information export to neocortex. However, these interpretations require further in vivo validation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C23, C77 represent interpretations and speculations based on the anatomical and electrophysiological findings. While the underlying data are solid, the functional implications for systems consolidation and memory remain speculative. The authors appropriately acknowledge the need for in vivo experiments. The claims are reasonable hypotheses but lack direct functional evidence.

results.result: Background claims establishing the context for the study, including the role of entorhinal layer V in hippocampal-cortical information transfer, the subdivision of layer V into LVa and LVb, functional differences between MEC and LEC, and the gap in knowledge regarding functional LVb-to-LVa connectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C20 are background statements supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims provide the scientific context and rationale for the study. C20 correctly identifies the knowledge gap that the current study addresses.

results.result: Discussion claims contextualizing findings within broader literature, including corroboration by other studies (Rozov et al., 2020), implications for grid cell populations, recurrent circuit mechanisms, and additional complexity from direct hippocampal projections to MEC LVa.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C78-C84 appropriately cite relevant literature to contextualize the findings. C53 provides important corroboration from an independent study. C80 and C82 are reasonable inferences from the connectivity data. C83 cites functional studies supporting the importance of layer III circuits. These discussion points appropriately integrate the current findings with existing knowledge.
